extracted.intended_audience: writers querying literary agents (aspiring and emerging authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing query letters and submission emails to literary agents and editors, including what to include, what to avoid, formatting, and submission etiquette for fiction and nonfiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized salutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each query has a personalized salutation—"Dear Mr. Jones" or "Dear Ms. Williams," etc. If unsure of an agent's gender, you can always use their full name: "Dear Cris Wendel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can further personalize by mentioning why you are submitting to this agent (e.g., referencing an interview or that they're seeking a particular subgenre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a strong hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a hook—an intriguing part/idea/element of your story that gets people's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the hook a cool, specific idea (examples given: 'three guys having a midlife crisis who decide to start a college fraternity' or 'Barbary pirates battling the British Navy...'). The hook should suck the reader in and make them want more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight unique quirks and plot points
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything unique or different or special about your main character and storyline should show up in a pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set your work apart from the many pitches an agent sees each week by stressing different/unique parts of your story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send requested sample pages as one attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't send an attachment for each chapter; one big attachment with all requested pages/chapters is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A blank page between chapter breaks is acceptable. Consolidate requested material into a single file unless the guidelines say otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: YA queries must foreground an appropriately aged protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: If you truly wrote a young adult (YA) novel, the main character is a teen (usually aged 16-18) and the pitch should start off with that teen and their life/goals/problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing adult characters upfront is a red flag indicating category confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualize each query email
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose an individual email for each agent you contact; do not send the same cut-and-paste message to dozens of agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic salutations or messages that remind the agent they are one of many recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not send exclusive queries (avoid asking for exclusivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive queries (submitting only to one agent) are not advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes individualized queries rather than exclusivity; follow agent-specific guidance if an agent explicitly requests exclusives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always send the first pages/chapters requested
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agent asks for '10 pages,' send the first 10 pages. Send pages from where the book begins—so from the prologue if you have one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prologue makes you nervous, consider whether it should be eliminated; do not try to hide or skip to later pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Gimmicks (offering money, sending cupcakes, hiring a singing telegram, etc.) are basically never advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stunts usually come off awkward or creepy; rely on a strong query letter and manuscript instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper submission channels and respect Twitter pitch norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit via email following agents' traditional submission guidelines; use Twitter pitch parties only on their scheduled days (e.g., #PitMad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't tweet agents unsolicited outside pitch events or use casual social-media approaches like 'Hey, I just finished a fantasy—you interested??' — don't be that writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction: bio optional; Nonfiction: platform/bio may be crucial
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're writing fiction, you do not need to have a bio; you can simply thank them. For nonfiction, who you are and your ability to sell the book (your platform) is often more important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have awards, publications, or relevant background, list such notes quickly and humbly.

rubrics_metrics.name: List notable publishing credits and awards succinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have publishing credits or awards, include them in your bio; they can help even if the query pitch is mediocre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name years and publishers and hyperlink to books if possible; mention brief notable facts (sales, awards, praise) so agents can learn more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose self-published status when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are querying a self-published book, you must disclose that it was self-published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiding it will harm trust later. If you've self-published other unrelated books, you do not have to mention those past books when pitching this new unrelated title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch one project at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitching more than one novel at a time can come off as scattershot; agents want one amazing project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't list multiple manuscripts in the same query; focus on the one project you want them to fall in love with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalities — be specific in your pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalities sink query letters; specifics bring them to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents receive many similar plots; concrete, specific details distinguish your pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow each agent's submission guidelines to the letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Always follow submission guidelines; agents want materials (query, synopsis, sample pages, proposal) sent in their desired way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to follow guidelines can result in your work not being considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce the main character in the present
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce your main character, in the present, to begin your query pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let readers get to know the MC and become invested before introducing backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on character over worldbuilding in query pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels are driven by characters; the agent needs to get to know at least your main character and begin to root for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave world-building, setting details, and secondary characters out of the query; that's acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent, professional formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pasted queries that show mismatched fonts (e.g., salutation different font than body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent formatting signals a generic cut-and-paste and takes the agent out of the moment. Keep fonts and formatting professional and uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use off-putting humor or casualness to pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid humor/levity or casual language in initial approaches if it undercuts professionalism (e.g., 'PEACE—ME OUT' style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal or flippant approaches are unlikely to help and can be counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send queries to the address specified in the guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agent's guidelines request submissions to queries@xyzagency.com, use that address rather than the agent's personal email you found elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the requested contact point shows professionalism and respect for agency workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: When citing why you're submitting to an agent, be specific about their past work
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing books/clients an agent represented is good, but name the books/clients you enjoyed — vague flattery hurts credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete references show genuine research and interest rather than empty name-dropping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the pitch concise (5–10 sentences) and avoid condensing the full synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches should be short — only 5–10 sentences. Do not try to squeeze the entire synopsis into the pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explaining too much or compressing the whole story; that should be in a synopsis, not the query pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ending the pitch with a rhetorical question
rubrics_metrics.description: Ending your pitch with a rhetorical question is an overused, ineffective technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close with a strong, declarative line or a concise hook rather than 'Wouldn't this be great?' style questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place bio at the end unless extraordinary or nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The bio section comes last in the query letter. Only lead with yourself if you have something extraordinary to say or are writing nonfiction where platform matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a previously adapted novel or major credentials can justify leading with the bio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the pitch's emotional tone to the book
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book is lighthearted and funny, make the agent laugh during the pitch; if it's disturbing horror, create a chilling effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to elicit the appropriate emotion rather than merely stating the book's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional in all communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism is expected; present your query as an application and avoid negative self-talk or unprofessional comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep language respectful, humble, and businesslike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why a self-published title deserves traditional publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When querying a self-published book, explain what makes the title deserving of a second life via traditional publishing rather than just linking to its Amazon page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide compelling reasons, sales data, audience, press, or other evidence that supports wider potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: For series, pitch only Book 1 and note series potential briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard protocol for a series is to pitch Book 1 and include a line like 'This is a standalone book, but could serve as the first in a series.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not explain what happens in all projected sequels; let the agent fall in love with the first book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlink and briefly annotate past published work
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have previously published books, name the years and publisher and hyperlink to the book; note brief notable facts like praise or sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep these mentions simple and sweet to allow the agent to learn more if interested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-deprecating or negative comments about yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking negatively about yourself (even humorously) in a query letter is not advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the query like an application; project competence and professionalism. Also, don't mention your age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference contemporary books, not only classics
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and reference books of today; in query letters, reference books that are current and relevant to today's market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to contemporary titles help agents place your book in the current marketplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query in small batches and iterate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not query your entire list at once. Query a small batch, evaluate responses (or lack thereof), revise query/pages if needed, then query the next batch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimizes risk of mass rejections and lets you refine your approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include social media handles and author platform links
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents like writers who are engaged in their communities online; include social media accounts (especially Twitter) in your query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place handles near signature (e.g., bottom-left after your signature) so agents can view your platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't brag about partial/full requests or use them prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agent asks to review your full manuscript, don't broadcast that to other agents as a brag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when you have a formal offer of representation can you notify other agents to prompt a response (handled politely and within a short timeframe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use offers of representation strategically and professionally
rubrics_metrics.description: If you receive a formal offer of representation, you may inform other agents reviewing your manuscript and give them a short deadline to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase communications professionally (e.g., 'I was offered representation by X and plan to decide within one week; please let me know if you'd like to review before then').

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell — use concrete sensory/detail-rich lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid bland summary lines ('David is depressed'); show specifics that paint pictures and evoke emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a vivid example (e.g., 'Ever since he lost his four-year-old son... he has spent far too much time staring at the bottom of empty glasses...') to demonstrate the difference between telling and showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write an informative, specific e-mail subject line
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a subject line that conveys important information (agent name, author name, genre, title) rather than generic 'Query'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Query for Christa - Sambuchino, thriller: DEAD MEN TELL NO TALES' is far more effective than 'Query' or 'Query - thriller'. Include the target agent's name if submitting to a generic agency address.
